one_liner: Hand-written AVX2 assembly for find, contains, min/max and argmin/argmax over plain arrays; claims to beat scalar compiler loops.
what_it_does: 52 x86-64 AVX2 assembly routines (NASM-syntax files under Linux/ despite the .s extension, MASM files under Windows/) plus fast-array-ops.h, which declares them extern "C" and adds C++ overloads FastContains, FastFind, FastMin, FastMax, FastMinIdx and FastMaxIdx for signed and unsigned 8- to 64-bit integers, float and double. The API takes a pointer and a count, not iterators: find returns the lowest matching index or ~0ULL, contains returns bool, and the min/max and index routines take a uint32_t count, with the index routines returning uint32_t. The project was earlier named FastExtrema.
how_it_is_fast: Large inputs run in 256-byte blocks: contains/find broadcast the query, OR together eight 32-byte vpcmpeq results and test once per block, and min/max keep eight independent vpmin/vminps accumulators; the tail is handled by re-running one overlapping final block rather than a scalar loop. Small inputs (below 32 to 256 elements depending on type) dispatch through a byte jump table to straight-line code for that size class. Argmin/argmax track per-lane best values plus a parallel index vector updated with vpcmpeq + vpblendvb, and the 8- and 16-bit versions nest 8/16/32-bit counters so narrow lanes do not overflow. The float/double min/max kernels reassociate the reduction, which compilers do only under -ffast-math, and that most likely explains the 28x and 14x rows.
when_to_use: Hot linear scans over contiguous arrays of plain integers on x86-64 CPUs that are guaranteed to have AVX2, e.g. membership tests on arrays of tens to a few hundred elements instead of a hash set (the README's main argument).
argmin/argmax over uint8/int8/int16 data, where the README claims its largest gains (35x and 19x) and compilers emit scalar code.
float/double min/max of data known to be NaN-free when you cannot enable -ffast-math for the whole translation unit.
Small array-backed priority queues or decrease-key structures whose operations reduce to find/min/argmin, as the README suggests.
GCC or Clang builds where you have measured std::find or std::min_element as the bottleneck and want a drop-in C ABI routine.
when_not_to_use: Data or queries that can be NaN: the float/double small-n find/contains paths report false matches and min/max/argmin results with NaN depend on element position.

Any target without AVX2 (no runtime dispatch or scalar fallback, so older x86 crashes with an illegal instruction), and AArch64 or other architectures; no macOS build either (symbols lack the leading underscore Mach-O expects).

MSVC builds: the MSVC STL already ships runtime-dispatched manual vectorization of find, min_element and max_element (including float and double) on x64/x86 by default, so measure std:: first; the README table is against scalar compiler output, not that.
Large DRAM-resident arrays, where the scan is memory-bound: a third-party Delphi wrapper timing 10M elements found the classical loop 'not so much different' (int64 min 13 ms vs 11 ms).
Arrays over 2^32 - 1 elements for the min/max/index routines (uint32_t count), or code that relies on std::min_element's first-index tie rule.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime; NASM to assemble the Linux/*.s files (NASM syntax: bits 64, yword, times db), ml64 (MASM) for Windows/*.asm
integration.min_toolchain: Any C++11 compiler for the header (<cstdint>, extern "C"); NASM or ml64 for the kernels; no build files, tests or CMake in the repo
integration.platforms: x86-64 only, AVX2 required (Haswell or later, Zen or later); System V (Linux) and Win64 ABIs
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; the routines only read caller memory and constant tables and keep no global state, so concurrent calls are safe by construction.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: pointer+count C API instead of iterators; find returns an index (~0ULL when absent) rather than an iterator; min/max index tie-breaking is unspecified (std::min_element returns the first); NaN and empty-array behavior differ

gotchas: NaN false matches (code bug, both Linux and Windows): FastFindFloat/FastFindDouble for n < 4 and FastContainsFloat/FastContainsDouble for n < 8 compare with vucomiss/vucomisd followed by je/sete/cmove and never check the parity flag, so an unordered compare counts as equal; a NaN element or NaN query reports a match (FastContainsFloat on {NaN, 2, 3} for query 5 returns true; FastFindFloat on {NaN, 1, 2} for query 1 returns 0), while the vector paths for larger n (vcmpeqps, ordered) never match NaN.

FastMin/FastMax for float and double return an all-ones NaN bit pattern on empty arrays (the accumulator is seeded with vpcmpeqd), not the min/max representable value the README promises; the integer versions do return INT_MAX/INT_MIN-style sentinels.

None of the 52 kernels executes vzeroupper, so they return with dirty upper YMM state; non-VEX SSE code that runs next (callers built without -mavx/-mavx2) pays AVX-SSE transition or false-dependency penalties on Intel cores, which a microbenchmark loop would not show.

The Windows MASM procedures that adjust rsp (e.g. sub rsp,104 in FastMinIdxI32.asm) are plain PROCs without FRAME/unwind directives, so a fault inside them cannot be unwound by SEH; the Linux sources are NASM-only and 11 of them still use bare-CR line breaks in their header lines (the 2025-12-11 commit normalized only FastFind64.s).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over argminmax (Rust crate, SSE to AVX-512 and NEON with 3-20x claimed vs scalar) only when you call from C or C++ on AVX2 x86 and also want find/contains for every integer width; over vectorized_find (AVX2 find experiments against std::find) because it covers min/max and argmin/argmax too. On MSVC, try the STL's own vectorized std::find and std::min_element before either.
verified_claims_summary: The only first-party numbers are the README's approximate large-n speedups over unnamed 'best compiler output' scalar loops (contains/find 7-22x, min/max element 1.1-28x, argmin/argmax 3.1-35x) with no CPU, compiler, flags, sizes or benchmark code, measured on code before the 2025-12-11 correctness fix. The one third-party data point (fatihtsp/FastArrayOps Delphi wrapper, 10M elements, CPU unstated) shows FastMin on an Int64 array at 11 ms versus a classical Delphi loop at 13 ms (about 1.2x, derived from page data).
status_note: Dormant from 2021 until a single 2025-12-11 bugfix commit (FastFind64 32-bit compare, 16-bit idx broadcast, U8 min-index sentinel); MIT and copyable, but it ships no tests, benchmark or build files and its float/double small-n paths still mishandle NaN, so vendor it only behind your own tests.
